name: After 1857: Crown Rule, Reformers and New Ideas

scenes.animation: A long winding road is painted across a map of India, starting at a milestone '1857' and ending at a far-off gate marked '1947'. Zippy zooms onto the road in running shoes, then stops, panting, at the first bend.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Ninety years? I thought freedom came in one big battle!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It was a long road, walked by millions of Indians in many different ways. Even before 1857 there were uprisings, like the Paika Sangram in Odisha and the long Sambalpur resistance.

scenes.animation: A timeline strip starts building along the road. Pin '1858': a scroll unrolls with a crown seal, labelled 'Royal Proclamation - Crown takes direct control from the East India Company'. Icons show a Secretary of State in London and a Viceroy in India, and about 560 small palaces labelled 'Princely states under paramountcy'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1858, the British Crown under Queen Victoria took direct control of India from the East India Company. India was now governed by the Secretary of State in London and the Viceroy in India.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A royal proclamation promised to respect some 560 Indian princes and to treat Indians like all other subjects.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Nice promises!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But they were not kept. Residents interfered in princely states, heavy taxes caused famines, and Indians were treated as inferior.

scenes.animation: Pin '1878' drops on the timeline: two stamped documents slam down, 'Arms Act - Indians cannot keep arms' and 'Vernacular Press Act - Indian-language papers censored'. A 'Europeans only' sign hangs on a railway carriage door.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Indians got lower pay than the British for the same posts and were kept out of clubs and some train carriages.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1878, the Arms Act banned Indians from keeping arms, and the Vernacular Press Act censored the Indian-language press.

scenes.animation: A row of postage stamps flips into view: Raja Ram Mohan Roy with 'Brahmo Samaj, 1828, Calcutta', Swami Dayananda Saraswati with 'Arya Samaj, 1875, Bombay', then Iswar Chandra Vidyasagar, Syed Ahmed Khan, and Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule with a schoolhouse icon for girls.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Meanwhile, reformers challenged child marriage, caste discrimination and the poor status of widows.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828, and Swami Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875. Vidyasagar, Syed Ahmed Khan and the Phules promoted education, especially for girls.

scenes.animation: A book titled 'Anandamath, 1882' opens and the words 'Vande Mataram, 1875' float up as music notes, which Tagore sings at a '1896 Congress' podium; a tag '1950: National Song' pins below. Then a young Swami Vivekananda stands at a Chicago podium with a '1893' banner and the quote 'Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Culture stirred national feeling too. Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay composed Vande Mataram in 1875 and placed it in his novel Anandamath in 1882. In 1950, it was adopted as India's National Song.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Swami Vivekananda's 1893 speech in Chicago defended India's civilisation. His call, arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached, inspired many freedom fighters.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: don't mix up the dates. The poem came in 1875, the novel in 1882.

scenes.animation: Pin '1885' drops on the timeline: 72 tiny delegates walk into a hall in Bombay labelled 'Indian National Congress - 1st session', with name tags for A.O. Hume, Dadabhai Naoroji and W.C. Bonnerjee (first president). A speech bubble reads 'Please, some reforms?'

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1885, the Indian National Congress held its first session in Bombay. A.O. Hume, Dadabhai Naoroji and W.C. Bonnerjee, its first president, played leading roles.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: At first, the Congress expressed loyalty to the British Crown and politely asked for reforms, but the government largely ignored it.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the timeline 1858-1885 glowing. Points appear: '1. 1858: Crown rule; promises broken', '2. Reformers and cultural voices: Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj, Vande Mataram, Vivekananda', '3. 1885: Congress founded, loyal and moderate at first'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: in 1858 the Crown took direct control, but its promises were broken.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: reformers, Bankim's Vande Mataram and Vivekananda awakened pride and self-confidence.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the Congress was founded in 1885 and began by asking for reforms.

name: Growing Discontent and the Partition of Bengal

scenes.animation: A cartoon map of Bengal gets sliced in two by giant British scissors labelled 'Curzon, 1905'. Across the cut, two hands reach out and tie a rakhi.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Why is that man cutting Bengal like a birthday cake?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That was the Partition of Bengal. But before we get there, see how anger had been building up.

scenes.animation: A map of India lights up region by region. Punjab: Kuka followers in white hand-spun clothes, tag 'Kuka Movement, Baba Ram Singh'. Maharashtra: a newspaper 'Kesari' and a Ganesh festival procession, tag 'Tilak'. Chota Nagpur: a bow and arrow, tag 'Birsa Munda, Ulgulaan 1899-1900'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In Punjab, Baba Ram Singh's Kuka Movement rejected foreign goods and British institutions, long before boycott became a national strategy.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In Maharashtra, Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote in his paper Kesari and turned Ganesh Chaturthi and the Shivaji festival into popular events. People called him Lokmanya.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the Chota Nagpur region, Birsa Munda led the Ulgulaan, the Great Tumult, in 1899-1900. He died in jail at just 24.

scenes.animation: Timeline pin '1905'. The Bengal map splits into a largely Muslim east and largely Hindu west with a label 'Divide and rule'. Crowds march singing Vande Mataram, a bonfire of foreign cloth blazes, and Indian-made cloth rolls out labelled 'Swadeshi'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1905, Viceroy Curzon partitioned Bengal. The official reason was better administration, but really it was divide and rule.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Leaders like Rabindranath Tagore and Surendranath Banerjee united people. Crowds sang Vande Mataram and tied rakhis as a sign of Hindu-Muslim unity.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two mass programmes began: Swadeshi, using Indian-made goods, and boycott of foreign goods. Bonfires of foreign cloth were lit in the streets.

scenes.animation: Timeline pin '1906' with three cards: the masthead of the daily 'Bande Mataram' with Bipin Chandra Pal and Aurobindo Ghose, the 'Bengal National College' with Aurobindo as principal, and a Calcutta Congress banner 'Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education'. A separate card flips up in Dhaka: 'All-India Muslim League, 1906'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1906, Bipin Chandra Pal launched the daily Bande Mataram, soon led by Aurobindo Ghose. It spread the goal of absolute national autonomy.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The same year, the Calcutta Congress adopted Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education as its objectives. In Dhaka, the All-India Muslim League was founded to defend Muslim political interests.

scenes.animation: Timeline pin '1907 Surat'. A Congress tent splits down the middle: one side labelled 'Moderates' with Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta, the other 'Nationalists' with the Lal-Bal-Pal trio and Aurobindo. A chair flies across as chaos erupts. An 'Exam Tip' sticker lands on the word 'Nationalists'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1907 at Surat, the Congress split. Moderates like Gokhale wanted gradual reforms within the Empire. Nationalists led by Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai and Aurobindo wanted nothing less than freedom.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So they were the Extremists?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That was the British and Moderate label. Exam tip: they called themselves Nationalists, since they saw nothing extreme in wanting independence.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the 1905-1907 timeline section highlighted. Points appear: '1. Discontent: Kukas, Tilak, Birsa Munda', '2. 1905 Partition of Bengal -> Swadeshi and boycott', '3. 1906 Swaraj demand, Muslim League; 1907 Surat split'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: discontent grew through the Kukas, Tilak and Birsa Munda.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the 1905 Partition of Bengal sparked Swadeshi and boycott.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: in 1906 Congress demanded Swaraj and the Muslim League was founded; in 1907 Congress split at Surat.

name: The Revolutionaries and the Home Rule Movement

scenes.animation: A newspaper stand shows four papers side by side: 'Voice of India' and 'The Bengalee' in calm grey, 'Kesari' and 'Bande Mataram' in orange, and 'Yugantar' in fiery red, smoking slightly. Zippy picks up the red one and his hair stands on end.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: This newspaper is practically on fire!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's Yugantar. Run by Barindra Ghose's group, linked to the Anushilan Samiti, it openly called for revolt. Some young Indians now chose the path of armed action.

scenes.animation: Timeline pin '1908'. A carriage at night, a flash, then a sketch of 18-year-old Khudiram Bose calm and smiling; flowers rain on a Calcutta funeral procession. A courtroom follows, labelled 'Alipore Bomb Trial', with Aurobindo in the dock, C.R. Das defending, and a stamp 'Acquitted'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1908, Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki threw bombs at a carriage they believed carried a harsh British judge, Kingsford. Prafulla shot himself; Khudiram, just 18, was hanged and became a national hero.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Aurobindo Ghose and many revolutionaries were then tried in the Alipore Bomb case. Defended by Chittaranjan Das, Aurobindo was acquitted.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The same year, Tilak was jailed in Mandalay for six years for sedition.

scenes.animation: The timeline extends: '1911 Partition of Bengal annulled; capital moved to Delhi', '1912 bomb at Viceroy Hardinge in Delhi', '1914-15 Ghadar Movement' with a ship sailing from North America to India. Portraits of Rash Behari Bose, Kartar Singh Sarabha and Bagha Jatin slide in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1911, the British withdrew the Partition of Bengal and shifted the capital to Delhi. In 1912, a bomb was thrown at Viceroy Hardinge there; he was injured but survived.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1914-15, the Ghadar Party, founded by Indians in North America, tried to spark a mutiny in the army during World War I. The plot was uncovered, and Kartar Singh Sarabha was executed at 19.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Bagha Jatin died in 1915 after a gun battle at Balasore while awaiting German arms.

scenes.animation: A dark building with rows of tiny cells appears on the Andaman Islands, labelled 'Cellular Jail - Kala Pani'. A prisoner turns a heavy oil press by hand. The scene then pans to northeast India with tags 'Tirot Sing, Khasi Revolt' and 'Rani Gaidinliu, Manipur'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: What happened to those who were caught?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Many were sent to the Cellular Jail in the Andamans, called Kala Pani, where prisoners faced solitary cells and brutal labour. It became a symbol of sacrifice.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Northeast resisted too, from Tirot Sing's Khasi Revolt to Rani Gaidinliu in Manipur, who fought the British from the age of 13.

scenes.animation: Timeline pin '1916 Lucknow'. The two halves of the torn Congress tent stitch back together; a handshake between a Congress figure and a Muslim League figure is labelled 'Lucknow Pact'. Tilak and Annie Besant raise a banner 'Home Rule: self-government within the Empire'. An 'Exam Tip' sticker lands on the banner.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Released in 1914, Tilak reunited the Congress at Lucknow in 1916. There, the Lucknow Pact brought the Congress and the Muslim League together.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The same year, Tilak and Annie Besant launched the Home Rule Movement for self-government within the British Empire.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: Home Rule meant self-government within the Empire, not full independence.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the 1908-1916 timeline stretch glowing. Points appear: '1. Revolutionaries: Khudiram Bose, Alipore trial, Ghadar, Bagha Jatin', '2. 1911: Bengal partition annulled; Kala Pani symbol of sacrifice', '3. 1916: Congress reunited, Lucknow Pact, Home Rule'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: revolutionaries like Khudiram Bose, the Ghadar fighters and Bagha Jatin risked everything.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Bengal's partition was annulled in 1911, and Kala Pani became a symbol of sacrifice.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: in 1916 the Congress reunited, signed the Lucknow Pact and backed Home Rule.

name: Gandhi, Non-Cooperation and the Fight for Purna Swaraj

scenes.animation: A spinning wheel turns slowly; the thread it spins stretches out across a map of India, tying villages together. Zippy tries to spin and gets tangled in the yarn.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: How can a spinning wheel fight an empire?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Through khadi, it became a symbol of self-reliance and a challenge to British cloth. Let's meet the man at the wheel.

scenes.animation: Timeline pin '1915': Gandhi steps off a ship from South Africa. Three local cards flip: 'Bihar - indigo farmers', 'Ahmedabad - mill workers', 'Kheda, Gujarat - peasants'. Beside them the word 'Satyagraha = insistence on truth' writes itself.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Mahatma Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 with his method of satyagraha, insistence on truth, based on non-violence.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He first used it for indigo farmers in Bihar, mill workers in Ahmedabad and peasants in Kheda.

scenes.animation: Timeline pin '1919'. A stamped paper 'Rowlatt Act - detention without trial' falls. The scene shifts to a walled garden in Amritsar on Baisakhi; the only exit is blocked by soldiers, and the screen fades to a sombre grey showing the Martyrs' Memorial. Captions: 'British count: nearly 400 dead', 'Indian estimates: over 1,000'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1919, the Rowlatt Act let police detain anyone without trial.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: On 13 April 1919, at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, General Dyer's troops sealed the exit and fired on an unarmed crowd. Indian estimates put the dead at over 1,000.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Rabindranath Tagore returned his British knighthood in protest.

scenes.animation: Timeline pins '1920 Nagpur' and '1922 Chauri Chaura'. People walk out of government schools and courts, carrying khadi; the Khilafat and Congress flags march side by side. Then a burning police station at Chauri Chaura, and Gandhi raising a hand to halt the movement.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1920, the Congress launched the Non-Cooperation Movement, boycotting foreign goods, schools and courts. It joined hands with the Khilafat Movement of the Ali brothers and Maulana Azad.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1922, after protesters burned a police station at Chauri Chaura, Gandhi called off the movement. Many leaders disapproved.

scenes.animation: Timeline pin '1928': black flags wave with the slogan 'Simon Go Back!'; Lala Lajpat Rai leads a peaceful march that is lathi-charged. Portraits of Bhagat Singh, Chandrashekhar Azad and Ashfaqulla Khan appear, and a pamphlet flutters down in the Assembly reading 'To make the deaf hear'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Simon Commission had no Indian member, so India shouted Simon Go Back. Lala Lajpat Rai died after a police lathi charge in 1928.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh and Chandrashekhar Azad chose force. Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged in 1931, aged just 22 to 23.

scenes.animation: Timeline pins '1929 Lahore' and '1930 Dandi'. Nehru reads the Purna Swaraj resolution on a dais. A dotted route draws 380 km south to the Gujarat coast, with marchers walking; Gandhi bends to pick up salt. Sarojini Naidu marches alongside. An 'Exam Tip' sticker pops up on 'Purna Swaraj'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In December 1929, the Congress at Lahore demanded Purna Swaraj, complete independence.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1930, Gandhi began the Civil Disobedience Movement with a 380-kilometre Salt March to Dandi, breaking the unfair salt law. Thousands of women joined.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: Purna Swaraj was demanded at the Lahore session of 1929. Don't confuse it with the Home Rule demand of 1916.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the 1915-1931 timeline glowing. Points appear: '1. Satyagraha; 1919 Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh', '2. 1920-22 Non-Cooperation with Khilafat; Chauri Chaura', '3. 1929 Purna Swaraj; 1930 Dandi March'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: Gandhi brought satyagraha, and 1919 saw the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Non-Cooperation joined with Khilafat, until Chauri Chaura in 1922.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: Purna Swaraj was demanded in 1929, and the Dandi March began in 1930.

name: From Quit India to Independence and Partition

scenes.animation: A clock tower shows almost midnight; the date '15 August 1947' glows. Beneath it, half the screen shows celebrating crowds with the tricolour, the other half shows crowded refugee trains with people on the roofs.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Freedom at midnight! Why does half the picture look so sad?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because freedom came with the pain of Partition. Let's see how we got there, starting in the 1930s.

scenes.animation: Timeline pins '1931 Gandhi-Irwin Pact', 'Poona Pact' and '1935 Government of India Act - provincial autonomy'. Gandhi and B.R. Ambedkar sit at a table; a scale labelled 'separate electorates' tips to 'more reserved seats'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1931, the Gandhi-Irwin Pact released non-violent prisoners, and the Congress joined a Round Table Conference in London, but it failed to produce a breakthrough.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: B.R. Ambedkar wanted separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. Gandhi feared this would divide Hindu society. The Poona Pact settled on more reserved seats instead.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1935, the British allowed elected provincial governments.

scenes.animation: Timeline pins '1939 World War II' and '1943 Azad Hind'. A map traces Subhas Chandra Bose's journey from India through Afghanistan and Russia to Germany, then by sea to Singapore; INA soldiers march towards Manipur and Nagaland. A grain sack is shipped away as a label 'Bengal famine, 1943' appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1939, India was dragged into World War II without being consulted. Over 2.5 million Indian soldiers served, and grain sent abroad worsened the 1943 Bengal famine.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Subhas Chandra Bose believed in armed struggle. He escaped in 1941, and in 1943 led the Indian National Army from Singapore, which fought in Manipur and Nagaland but was defeated.

scenes.animation: Timeline pin '1942'. Crowds carry 'Quit India' banners; the words 'Do or Die' blaze across the screen. Aruna Asaf Ali hoists a flag at Gowalia Tank Maidan, and 17-year-old Kanaklata Barua leads a flag procession in Gohpur, Assam.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After rejecting the Cripps Mission, Gandhi launched the Quit India Movement in August 1942 with the call, do or die.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Leaders were arrested, but people kept going. Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag in Bombay, and Kanaklata Barua was killed at 17 leading a flag march in Assam.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Viceroy called it the most serious rebellion since 1857.

scenes.animation: Timeline pins '1946: Air Force and Navy mutinies, Cabinet Mission, Direct Action Day' and '1947: Radcliffe Line'. A red line draws itself through Punjab and Bengal, creating India, West Pakistan and East Pakistan. Sardar Patel then fits scattered princely-state jigsaw pieces into one map of India. An 'Exam Tip' sticker lands on the Radcliffe Line.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1946, mutinies in the Royal Indian Air Force and Navy showed Britain it could no longer rely on its Indian forces. Jinnah's Direct Action Day brought terrible communal violence to Calcutta.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1947, Cyril Radcliffe was given just five weeks to draw the border splitting Punjab and Bengal. Millions migrated amid horrific violence.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sardar Patel integrated over 560 princely states, earning the name Iron Man of India.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: remember freedom came from many forces together, not one person or one method.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the complete 1858-1947 timeline glowing end to end. Points appear: '1. Many paths: Moderates, Nationalists, revolutionaries, Gandhian satyagraha', '2. 1942 Quit India; INA and 1946 mutinies shook British rule', '3. 15 August 1947: independence, with the tragedy of Partition'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: freedom came through many paths, Moderates, Nationalists, revolutionaries and Gandhi's satyagraha.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Quit India, the INA and the 1946 mutinies showed Britain its rule could not last.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: India became free on 15 August 1947, but Partition left a deep scar.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: A long road, and a collective victory.
